_expect.name: White Owl Face and Laughing Owl Area

nh_white_owl_face_and_laughing_owl_area.blurb: This is the right-hand end of the Left Cliff at Owl's Cliff, in the Kancamagus country of the central White Mountains. Two distinct faces share the zone. The steep, sheer White Owl Face holds short one-pitch test pieces in the low 5.11s to 5.13, finger cracks and thin bolted faces among them. Around the corner, a tall buttress of vertical cracks plus a slab to its right gives easier, friendlier climbing, from 5.6 up to a stiff 5.10. The 13 routes are mostly trad, with a handful of sport lines and one top rope, on granite. A stick clip helps with some high first bolts.

nh_5_humphrey_s_hollow.blurb: Humphrey's Hollow is a scatter of small crags along the far right side of Humphrey's Ledge, a short drive from North Conway. It offers pleasant single-pitch climbing at modest grades: roughly 13 routes, mostly trad with five or so bolted lines, running from an easy 5.5 up to a single 5.12, with the bulk between 5.6 and 5.10. It makes a good quieter alternative to the big, busy ledges nearby, and suits a party wanting a relaxed day of moderate leads rather than a committing wall.

nh_06_the_dark_side.blurb: The Dark Side is among the steepest walls on Dickey Ledge, the long cliff above the Welch-Dickey hiking loop near Thornton and Waterville Valley. A prominent chimney and off-width splits the wall, and the rest is a mix of cracks, corners and face climbing on granite. Of its 13 routes, nearly all are trad, with a single bolted line; the few bolts that exist do not make it a sport crag, so bring a standard rack. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, with most of the climbing in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. Reach the base by hiking up the trail and then either rappelling in or following a climbers' path below the corners.

_expect.name: Jeremy's Wall - Main Cliff upper right

nh_jeremy_s_wall_main_cliff_upper_right.blurb: Jeremy's Wall is the upper-right section of the Main Cliff at Russell Crags, a bolted sport area in the Lincoln and Woodstock part of the White Mountains. The 13 sport routes stand side by side, around 100 feet long, and range from steep, powerful moves to technical footwork on lower-angle rock. The grades lean hard: one 5.7, a few 5.11s, and mostly 5.12 and 5.13. The cliff has broad mountain views and is visible from the highway. The approach is steep, with a gully, switchbacks and fixed ropes, and the final scramble onto the main ledge calls for care. Stick clips are handy for first bolts.
